extracted.intended_audience: administrative law practitioners, tribunal members, policymakers, and scholars concerned with unemployment insurance appeal procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards governing the conduct, decision-writing, limits, and appellate pathways of Boards of referees and the Umpire in unemployment insurance appeals (Canadian context). Covers procedural powers, required content of decisions, referral and adjournment rules, recording and distribution, and reopening/reconsideration standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of internal UIC documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC has no objection to its internal documents (e.g., the UIC Manual and the Medical Yardsticks) being consulted by Boards of referees, but requests that they not be cited in support of their decisions and that the Boards base their reasoning strictly on the Act, the Regulations and the caselaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may consult internal materials for assistance, but must not rely on or cite them as authoritative grounds for decisions; legal reasoning must be drawn from statute, regulations and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording of proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of the Boards of referees, and particularly the examination proceedings, are not normally recorded; reg. 182(2) refers to the 'report of the proceedings' but in practice no such report is compiled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only appeals concerning labour disputes are typically recorded and transcribed verbatim because they are considered sufficiently complex; otherwise the only documentary evidence is submissions, written observations, and the Board's written decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referral powers for unresolved factual issues (reg. 181)
rubrics_metrics.description: If factual aspects essential to the decision cannot be conclusively established, the chairman of the Board is empowered by reg. 181 to refer the question to the UIC for investigation and report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When questions of insurable employment or contributions arise they must be referred to the Minister of National Revenue under sec. 105 of the Act; referrals and investigations may interrupt the hearing and may lead to a differently constituted Board at resumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjournment authority and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: If the appellant notifies inability to attend, to arrange representation, or to prepare his case in time, the chairman grants an adjournment to a date to be fixed by the clerk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjournments are routine for appellant unavailability; parties should expect possible change in panel composition due to rotation of referees (reg. 178(3)) and availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available dispositions of the Board
rubrics_metrics.description: At the conclusion of examination the Board of referees must consider one of four possible courses of action: adjourn the hearing, confirm the Agent II's decision, rescind it, or amend it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the exclusive practical outcomes following examination; the Board's power to amend is subject to further legal limits (see 'ultra petita' and sanctions limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ultra petita / limits on altering parties' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In confirming or amending a decision, an appellate body may not go beyond the claims of the parties (rule of ultra petita).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards must confine remedies and findings to the scope of the parties' claims; they cannot grant relief or impose obligations that the parties did not seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on imposing sanctions (disqualifications and penalties)
rubrics_metrics.description: With regard to disqualifications (sec. 40 and 41) and penalties (sec. 47) the Board may not impose sanctions harsher than those imposed by the Agent, except in exceptional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: the Board may impose sanctions where the Agent has not, if (1) knowledge of this aspect materially affects the decision regarding the question raised by the appeal and (2) the Agent could not have known of it when he made his decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope for considering overpayments/disentitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: When the UIC declares a claimant retroactively disentitled to benefit, the Board is authorized to consider this decision only if the appellant challenges the disentitlement on which the overpayment is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimant's appeal is strictly about inability to pay, the Board has no grounds to review the UIC's discretionary decision to write off debt; the Board can only indirectly cancel or reduce debt by rescinding or amending the Agent II's decision regarding entitlement and may recommend the UIC write off debt (reg. 175(1)(e)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision must be based on legal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's decision should be based on legal reasoning — it should apply standards taken from the Act, the Regulations and the caselaw to the situation of the appellant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A referee's personal disagreement with the law or sense of injustice does not justify a decision that does not conform to the law; this applies equally to minority and majority decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation confidentiality and decision drafting procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Once examination is completed the Board should deliberate in camera (appellant, witnesses, UIC officials, and clerk not present), attempt consensus, and then dictate or write its decision; the chairman leads and moderates the discussion and consults colleagues on exact wording when dictating to the stenographer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If consensus cannot be reached, reasons for disagreement should be clearly identified; any member may write a separate or minority decision following the same format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to record decision in writing (sec. 94(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec. 94(2) requires the Board of referees to record its decision in writing using a UIC form showing names of appellant, intervenors, witnesses, representative, presence/representation of appellant, date and place of hearing, followed by the decision and signatures of agreeing members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written decision form normally includes an indication of applicable sections of the Act, a description of evidence brought after the submission, a summary of facts where necessary, an assessment of facts in light of the law, and the operative decision (confirm/rescind/amend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Content elements of a Board decision
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board decision typically includes: (1) an indication of the sections of the Act applicable; (2) a description of evidence brought to the Board subsequent to the submission; (3) a summary of the facts where necessary; (4) an assessment of the facts in the light of the law; and (5) the decision confirming, rescinding or amending the Agent's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assessment of facts in light of the law is the crucial element and must be adequately justified to enable effective appeal to the Umpire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, logic and simplicity in style
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions should be presented to affected members of the public with clarity, logic and simplicity; however, referees' reasoning is often cryptic and terse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairmen with legal training may produce clearer legal style and reasoning; inadequate explanations (e.g., only two short sentences) can impede the claimant's right of appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate hearing time and avoidance of excessive brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings are scheduled at half-hour intervals in theory but in practice take at least an hour when the appellant is present; the Umpires have objected to excessive brevity of hearings before Boards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairman should cut short discussion only when appellant has nothing significant to add but must generally ensure appellant's opportunity to state the case is not restricted; appellants are often timid rather than abusive of the right to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-disclosure of decision at conclusion of hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision of the Board of referees is never revealed immediately to the appellant; the chairman informs the appellant it will be mailed, and referees must avoid giving any hints about their decision or its effect on benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clerk is responsible for mailing the decision to the appellant and for sending copies to interested third parties, the Agent, the chairman, and the UIC Regional Office along with the submission (fulfilling reg. 182(3) and (4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on distribution and non-publication of decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of Boards of referees are sent only to the appellant, interested third parties, the Agent, the chairman, and the UIC Regional Office; they are not published and do not become part of the caselaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should not expect Board decisions to be precedential in the published caselaw; distribution is strictly limited by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal information to be provided with decision notice
rubrics_metrics.description: The back of the form notifying the appellant of the decision must print the main elements of the procedure for an appeal to the Umpire: rights of appeal (sec. 95 and reg. 184(1)), time limits for filing an appeal, rights of interested third parties to submit opinions, the right to request a hearing before the Umpire, and the obligation upon claimant or employer to obtain permission in advance from the chairman of the Board of referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures appellants and interested parties are informed of procedural rights and time limits for further review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural regularity — irregularities can vitiate decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board's decision may be vitiated by an irregularity in form (example: UIC convened a second Board on the ground the original decision was vitiated by an irregularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural defects can prompt re-hearings and may lead to controversial outcomes; ensuring form and procedure conformity is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate legal effect and consequences for payments/overpayments
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision of the Board of referees has immediate effect for benefits: the claimant is reinstated as of the effective date unless the Board specifies a more recent date; however, if the Umpire later reinstates the initial decision, payments made pursuant to the Board are considered duly paid and overpayments are recoverable from the claimant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should be aware that successful Board decisions can create interim payment consequences that may later result in overpayments if reversed on further appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agent's power to amend decisions on new facts (sec. 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sec. 102 allows the Agent to amend his decision, even if upheld by the Board, if he discovers a change in the claimant's situation or facts unknown to the claimant at the time of the initial decision or the Board's decision; the Agent must give the claimant the opportunity to present arguments before the Board of referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments by the Agent based on new facts may lead to a 'retrial' before a differently constituted Board; the claimant must be afforded opportunity to be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: UIC's power to re-open files and reclaim payments (secs. 57 and 102)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secs. 57 and 102 authorize the UIC to re-open a claimant's file within 36 months after the payment of the last benefit and reclaim any money to which he was not entitled, but the UIC must present new facts — elements discovered which normal vigilance would not have enabled it to discover at the proper time (CUB 3840).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reopening is permitted only on demonstrably 'new' facts not discoverable by ordinary diligence; this limits arbitrary retroactive recoveries.
